correctness.rationale: The exponent differences generate the full lattice and the convex hull is the \(5\times5\) square. The six homogenized sections have bidegree \((5,5)\) with no base point, and the dense-torus inverse \(y=z_3/z_2\), \(x=z_2^3/(z_0z_3^2)\) proves birationality. Each facet contains only its two endpoints, separated by lattice length five, so the boundary restriction is a fifth-power map. Thus the normalization is \(\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\), generic boundary fibers have five points, the boundary is singular and the dense torus is smooth. The degree is the normalized square area, equivalently \((5H_1+5H_2)^2=50\). A fresh arithmetic replay reproduced the lattice-generation, four facet lengths and degree.
correctness.risk: No scheme-theoretic conductor or analytic corner type is claimed.

originality.rationale: The object-specific arithmetic is correct, but the final geometric package is a direct specialization of standard projective toric normalization theory. Cox-Little-Schenck Theorem 3.A.5 states that the normalization of \(X_A\) is the toric variety of the normal fan of \(\operatorname{Conv}(A)\); for this square that is \(\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\). Classical toric branch theory states that the normalization separates a number of branches equal to the face-lattice index; every edge here has index five. The degree of a projective toric variety is the normalized volume. Those general results, plus the six published exponents, implication-wise determine the submitted normalization, degree and generic boundary branching; smoothness of the dense torus and closedness then give the stated singular locus. Exact wording in the SONC paper is unnecessary for coverage.
